newsitem.title: UK: UK Conservative govt faults Labour's budget plans.
newsitem.headline: UK Conservative govt faults Labour's budget plans.

text.p: Britain's ruling Conservative Party said on Tuesday that it had found more than 12 billion pounds worth of "black holes" in the main opposition Labour Party's spending plans.

Presenting a Conservative Research Department paper, Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke said the gaps in Labour's financing plans came to 5.3 billion stg in 1997/98 and seven billion in 1998/99.
"This gives a total of 12.37 billion (stg) that Labour would have to raise through extra taxes or borrowing over the two-year period," the document said.
The Conservatives identified four types of "black hole" in Labour's plans.
-- If Labour was to keep, as it has vowed, to the government's spending plans for the next two years, it would have to carry out Conservative reforms already factored in to the budget forecasts.
These include future privatisations, reforms of social security and extending the Private Finance Initiative in the Naitional Health Service. The government said Labour oppose these policies.
-- Labour has incorrectly assumed that some of its policy commitments would not increase public spending and the budget deficit, the Conservative document said.
These include the release of local authority receipts for house building,the extension of student loans and extra spending on school repairs.
-- Labour is also wrong to say that the employment measures it plans to fund through a windfall tax on privatised utilities will not add to public spending, the Conservatives said.
Moreover, the actual cost of these measures would be much higher than the three billion pounds ($4.88 billion) price tag Labour has put on the schemes.
-- Labour has committed itself to reduce value added tax on fuel, currently levied at eight percent, but has so far only explained how it would make up for part of the loss of revenue.
